problem: Prior LVLM-robot integrations rely on pre-mapped spaces, hand-crafted state representations (JSON scene graphs, selected images), reduced action spaces and fixed control logic, so they are myopic, brittle and do not generalize to new tasks.
motivation: Modern robotic stacks already offer rich perception, reasoning and navigation capabilities, and LVLMs now have strong function-calling and agentic abilities. Casting the LVLM as a controller that invokes these modules could yield task-agnostic navigation in unmapped environments.
key_idea: Give an LVLM agent a tool library (perception, reasoning utilities, navigation) plus a multimodal memory, and let it generate and execute its own task-specific workflow via self-discover-style planning.
insight: Visual and spatial memory matter most: removing all rasterized representations drops accuracy from 77% to 10% correct, and removing the occupancy grid raises inconclusive runs to 52%. Structured self-discover workflow generation is crucial: plain chain-of-thought falls to 7% correct with 69% time-limit failures. The agent's path is much shorter than EuC's, but token cost is very high.
method: Agent tuple: ARNA = (stack S, tool interface Γ, LVLM L, workflow Π, memory M, task T); the LVLM generates and executes a task-specific workflow instead of a fixed pipeline.

Robotic toolset: perception tools (get_images, query_scene_graph, occupancy grid), reasoning utilities (shortest path, visibility, reachability, LVLM-generated custom functions) and navigation tools (goto with A*, rotate, follow_path, LVLM-based explore_frontiers).

Multimodal memory: LVLM-editable text (findings, spatial descriptions, auto action log) plus a top-down occupancy grid annotated with landmarks, updated after every step and after each navigation segment.

Workflow generation: modified self-discover in four stages (select heuristic, adapt, pseudocode, implement with tools/control flow/custom functions), applied recursively; also produces open-set perception targets and termination conditions zero-shot.

Execution loop: the LVLM picks the next plan step, in any order and repeatable, from memory; navigation goals go to the motion stack, and the resulting observation sequence updates memory. The workflow is not revised online.
Perception stack: scene graph updated online with Grounding DINO, rooms segmented with GPT-4o-mini; GPT-4o is the LVLM.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen, prompted); Grounding DINO for open-set detection; GPT-4o-mini for room segmentation
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D with pose, aggregated into a 3D scene graph and occupancy grid
setting.action_space: high-level tool calls (goto(x,y,z) with A*, rotate, follow_path, explore_frontiers) over the occupancy map
setting.privileged: none (unmapped environment, explores online); budget limits of 500 steps or $5

numbers.extra: Accuracy printed as Correct/Incorrect; remaining 9% inconclusive (500 steps or $5 budget); mean token usage 673.11k

numbers.eval_set_note: 30 episodes (split not stated in the paper; val-unseen assumed)
numbers.extra: not designed for the task; qualitative/limited evaluation
numbers.evidence: On 30 episodes, our model achieved a 12% success rate

numbers_note: HM-EQA has no official split label in the paper. The RxR-CE split is unspecified; only SR on 30 episodes is given.
results: On HM-EQA, ARNA (GPT-4o) reaches 77% correct / 14% incorrect, beating EuC-GPT-4o (61/39) and the pre-mapped OpenEQA Multi-Frame VLM (CLIP) (66/34). Its mean path length is 16.55 m versus 175.91 m for EuC-GPT-4o, though it uses far more tokens (673k). It reaches 12% SR on 30 RxR-CE episodes.
limitations: Very high compute and cost: 30–60 minutes and $1–3 per task, 673k tokens per episode, with sequential API calls.
Relies on strong LVLMs and careful prompts; GPT-4o-mini fails, and there is no plan or workflow re-planning or memory verification.
Weak on RxR-CE (12% SR on 30 episodes); the main quantitative evidence is a single benchmark, HM-EQA.
compares_to: OpenEQA baselines (Blind, Scene-Graph, Frame Captions, Multi-Frame VLM)
